From Middle English choken (also cheken), from earlier acheken, from Old English āċēocian (“to choke”), probably derived from Old English ċēoce, ċēace (“jaw, cheek”), see cheek. Cognate with Icelandic kok (“throat”), koka (“to gulp”). See also achoke.
Back-formation from artichoke.

senses.d: To be unable to breathe because of obstruction of the windpipe (for instance food or other objects that go down the wrong way, or fumes or particles in the air that cause the throat to constrict).
ex: Ever since he choked on a bone, he has refused to eat fish.
Lenore began to choke with the fine dust and to feel her eyes smart and to see it settle on her hands and dress.

senses.d: To prevent (someone) from breathing or talking by strangling or filling the windpipe.
ex: The collar of this shirt is too tight; it’s choking me.
With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder:

senses.d: To obstruct (a passage, etc.) by filling it up or clogging it.
ex: to choke a cave passage with boulders and mud
But at Christmas the pavements were crowded with overdressed shoppers from the country, the streets choked with slow but strident traffic.

senses.d: To hinder or check, as growth, expansion, progress, etc.; to kill (a plant by robbing it of nutrients); to extinguish (fire by robbing it of oxygen).
ex: And some [seeds] fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them:
I have cut maize stalks or green plants with which he means to choke the flames.

senses.d: To perform badly at a crucial stage of a competition, especially when one appears to be clearly winning.
ex: He has a lot of talent, but he tends to choke under pressure.
“I can’t say that I choked on those match points,” Williams said. “She literally played her best tennis ever on those shots.”

senses.d: To move one's fingers very close to the tip of a pencil, brush or other art tool.
To hold the club or bat lower on the shaft in order to shorten one's swing.
ex: Take a grip with your right hand, slightly choked down from your normal grip.

senses.d: To be checked or stopped, as if by choking
ex: […] the words choked in his throat.
Speech choked in Eugene’s throat.

senses.d: To check or stop (an utterance or voice) as if by choking.
ex: A hundred times fain he would have spoke, but still his rising Passion choak’d his Words;
At that I opened my mouth to speak, and found a hoarse phlegm choked my voice.

senses.d: To have a feeling of strangulation in one's throat as a result of passion or strong emotion.
ex: Grobstock began to choke with chagrin.

senses.d: A control on a carburetor to adjust the air/fuel mixture when the engine is cold.
In wrestling, karate (etc.), a type of hold that can result in strangulation.
A constriction at the muzzle end of a shotgun barrel which affects the spread of the shot.
A partial or complete blockage (of boulders, mud, etc.) in a cave passage.
A choking coil.
A major mistake at a crucial stage of a competition because one is nervous, especially when one is winning.
The mass of immature florets in the centre of the bud of an artichoke.

Reshaping of earlier choregraphy, a borrowing from French chorégraphie, from Ancient Greek χορεία (khoreía, “dance”) + -γραφίᾱ (-graphíā, “written form (of a word, etc.), spelling”). By surface analysis, choreo- + -graphy. Both choregraphy and choreography replaced earlier chorography in the dance sense (from χορός (khorós, “dance ring, round dance”) + -γραφία (-graphía); compare Greek χορογραφία (chorografía)), which had been used in 1710 as a translation of the same French term.
